models.summary: Health is a weighted count of passes. Fourteen indicators under six factors are each scored one if they fall inside a health range and zero otherwise, and the overall point gain is the weighted sum. AHP sets the weights: investment 0.4615, access 0.2402, education 0.1095, research 0.1095, equity 0.0515, attraction 0.0515, with CR 0.0416. Positive indicators take their lower bound at the 80 percent quantile, negative ones their upper bound, and the two two-sided indicators, GPI and employment, are bounded from a normal distribution that passes a K-S test at 0.05. Only a score of one is fully healthy. The grades step down at 0.9, 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2.
models.purpose: Turn each indicator into a pass or fail and grade the system by the weighted share of passes.
objectives: Grade a system and point at the indicators that fail.

details: Fifty countries, 2009 to 2018. Fourteen indicators, six factors.
Health share fixed at 0.8 from QS rankings. Net student flow bounded below by zero. K-S test at alpha 0.05.

parameter_estimation.method: AHP with a stated priority order, consistency-tested. Health bounds from sample quantiles, and from a normal fit for the two two-sided indicators.

algorithm.description: Build the comparison matrix, test it, read the weights, set the ranges, score each indicator, sum.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The score is reproducible from the bits and the weights. The ranges depend on a sample the paper does not tabulate.

constraints: Fifty countries with relatively complete systems.
Full health only at a score of one.
strengths: A failure stays visible, because each indicator is a bit.
The two-sided indicators are tested for normality instead of forced into a quantile.
limitations: The 80 percent healthy share is taken from QS and not derived.
The priority order behind the matrix is the authors' judgment.
missing_details: The raw sample behind the quantiles.
The per-indicator weights inside each factor, beyond the figure.
assumptions: Health depends only on these indicators.
The sample shares the population distribution.
A health interval exists for every indicator.

models.summary: Sustainability is read from a productivity trend. CCR efficiency is the best weighted ratio of outputs to inputs, and a unit is efficient when that ratio reaches one. Because CCR ignores productivity change, the Malmquist form compares adjacent years. DEAP computes the ratios. Setting the first year to one builds the path. A system is unsustainable after three consecutive declines in five years, poor after two, and highly sustainable after at most one.
models.purpose: Judge whether a system keeps its effectiveness, from the run of year-to-year efficiency.
objectives: Classify sustainability from consecutive declines in efficiency.

parameter_estimation.method: Weights are solved inside the program, not set in advance. DEAP computes the Malmquist ratios.

algorithm.description: Solve the CCR program per year, take Malmquist ratios between adjacent years, chain them from a base of one, count consecutive declines.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Optimum exists and the ratio is bounded by one.

details: US steady and rising. Germany entirely rising. India down for four adjacent years. UK called poor, Japan sustainable.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The rule is clear. The ratios behind the figures are not printed, so the counts cannot be rechecked.

constraints: Same indicator set as the health model.
Declines counted only inside the last five years.
strengths: No weights are chosen by hand.
The rule allows a dip and judges the recovery.
limitations: The Malmquist formula is described, not written.
The three-year and two-year cutoffs are unexplained.
assumptions: Decision variables are inputs and reflection variables are outputs.
The first year can be set to one without loss.

models.summary: Policy sets direction but not speed, so the effect is random. Each year the implementation is good, poor, or counterproductive. The effect and a buffer are normal random variables whose mean shifts with the gap from the healthy value and with last year's state. The indicator updates by multiplying by one minus their sum. Twenty runs put employment at its bound in about ten years and enrollment in about thirteen. Net student flow normalizes in about 48 years. The count of institutions is discrete and is handled by targets instead.
models.purpose: Forecast how fast an unhealthy indicator reaches its healthy bound under a policy whose speed is uncertain.
objectives: Time the arrival of each main indicator at its healthy bound.

details: India. Employment starts near 60 percent, enrollment near 29 percent. Twenty independent runs.
Healthy bounds from the health model. Convergence to the normal value is assumed.
The chain is built to converge, but no fixed point is derived.

parameter_estimation.method: The means and variances in Table 4 are chosen, not estimated. k differs by indicator and is not tabulated.

algorithm.description: Draw the effect and the buffer from normals shifted by the gap and last year's state, update the indicator, repeat, average over twenty runs.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Assumed. Policies are adjusted when the effect fades near the bound.

details: Employment reaches its bound in about 10 years, enrollment in about 13, net flow in about 48. Timeline: 2018, 2028, 2031, 2066, 2118.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The averages are reported from the runs. The code in the appendix uses a fixed k of 0.0017 and a normal value of 77, so only one indicator is reproducible from what is printed.

constraints: Next state depends only on the current state and value.
The institution count is excluded as discrete.
strengths: The randomness is motivated: speed is unknown, direction is not.
The push weakens as the indicator nears its bound, which avoids overshoot by assumption.
limitations: The printed rule puts both thresholds at 0.05, leaving no room for the middle state.
missing_details: The value of k per indicator.
The transition probabilities, which are sampled rather than written.
assumptions: One of three states occurs each year.
A policy that worked is easier next year.
Unhealthy indicators eventually reach normal values.
